title: Deterministic Hypergraph SYK: Melonic Dominance and Maximal Chaos Without Disorder Averaging
abstract: We show that SYK-like melonic solvability and maximal chaos survive in a sparse deterministic model, without disorder averaging. Our deterministic hypergraph SYK model (hSYK) consists of $N$ Majorana fermions on a $q$-uniform, $d$-regular interaction hypergraph with only $O(dN)$ interaction terms and uniform positive couplings. Under explicit geometric and spectral expansion conditions, its two-point function satisfies the standard melonic Schwinger-Dyson equation up to $O(d^{-1})$ corrections, while the leading bilocal effective action coincides with that of ordinary SYK at the dominant large-$d$ saddle. Its connected four-point function factorizes into a temporal SYK ladder kernel and a line-graph random walk. A finite line-graph spectral gap controls the visibility of the maximally chaotic uniform mode in generic localized OTOCs and, by gapping non-uniform spatial modes in the bilocal spectrum, excludes additional light fluctuation modes beyond the Schwarzian. Exact diagonalization further shows melonic two-point scaling, single-instance Wigner-Dyson statistics, and the predicted graph-controlled spatial decay of OTOCs. The model therefore offers a disorder-free realization of the essential melonic and chaotic features of SYK, in a form more amenable to quantum simulation.
summary: This paper constructs a deterministic hypergraph realization of the SYK model, aiming to show that its characteristic chaotic and melonic physics does not require random disorder averaging. By analyzing the two-point function and OTOCs using advanced techniques like the cavity formalism, the authors demonstrate that the model successfully reproduces the key theoretical predictions of SYK in a structured, non-random setting.
main_problem: To determine if the essential melonic and chaotic features of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model can be realized in a sparse, deterministic setting without relying on disorder averaging.
main_result: The deterministic hypergraph SYK model (hSYK) successfully recovers the standard SYK bilocal effective action and exhibits characteristic chaotic signatures like Wigner-Dyson statistics, providing a disorder-free realization.
method: The analysis uses Schwinger-Dyson equations, the cavity formalism, and spectral expansion techniques to evaluate correlation functions in the large-$d$ limit.
model_or_system: The model is a deterministic hypergraph SYK (hSYK) defined on a $q$-uniform, $d$-regular interaction hypergraph with $N$ Majorana fermions. The interactions are sparse, scaling as $O(dN)$ rather than exponentially.
key_observables: Two-point function, connected four-point function, Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs), and spectral statistics (Wigner-Dyson).
important_parameters: Large-$d$ limit, fixed $q \ge 4$, and the structural constraints imposed by the hypergraph geometry.
main_assumptions: The model relies on structural axioms concerning the hypergraph, such as the 'one-overlap' condition ($|e_a \cap e_b| \le 1$) and spectral separation gaps.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the physical hypergraph, its line graph, and the relationship between these structures.
paper_structure: The paper develops the analysis by first establishing the two-point function via the Schwinger-Dyson equation and cavity formalism, then deriving the effective action, and finally confirming chaotic features using OTOCs and spectral statistics.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, geometrically constrained, and disorder-free platform to study universal quantum chaotic dynamics (like those seen in SYK), which is highly relevant for understanding strongly correlated quantum matter.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three representations of a 4-uniform, 2-regular hypergraph. We present an example with |E| = 5, N = 10. (a) The physical hypergraph, where each interaction ei contains exactly q = 4 fermions. Because d = 2, every black dot lies in exactly two colored regions. (b) The line graph is fully connected (K5) because every pair of hyperedges shares exactly one fermion. (c) The bipartite Levi graph makes the parameters obvious: uniformity implies that every top node (interaction) has degree q = 4, while regularity implies that every bottom node (fermion) has degree d = 2. (Note B(H) has many cycles, so this example may not be representative of a hypergraph satisfying Axiom 2.)

Figure 2: The two geometric axioms that must be satisfied by the hypergraph. (a) The 1-overlap condition forbids hyperedges from sharing multiple fermions. (b) The Levi sparsity axiom restricts the bipartite Levi graph (hyperedges as squares, fermions as circles). A valid model is locally tree-like. The red edges illustrate extra connections beyond the spanning tree (black), yielding a local cycle rank (mLevi) of 2. We require the density of these local cycles to remain bounded by O(1) in the limit d ≫1.

Figure 3: Schematic cavity geometry after deleting a distinguished hyperedge, shown for q = 4. (a) A radius-R neighborhood around e in the Levi graph contains four rooted branches together with O(1) short cycle-closing reconnections (dashed red). (b) Deleting e and pruning these defects produces a spanning forest with disjoint rooted neighborhoods. (c) At fixed perturbative order, couplings between distinct rooted trees require at least two additional hyperedge insertions and are therefore O(d−1).

Figure 4: Leading large-d melonic Schwinger-Dyson equation, shown schematically. The left-hand side contains the kinetic and contact terms for Gij(τ, τ ′). The right-hand side is the melonic self-energy contribution: a sum over hyperedges e ∋i and intermediate time t, with q−1 site-diagonal propagators dressing the full line Gji(τ ′, t).

Figure 5: Diagrammatic origin of the site-space kernel K, shown schematically for q = 4. (a) The diagonal propagator is decomposed as Gi = G+δGi. (b) The leading large-d self-energy Σi is obtained by summing over hyperedges e ∋i. (c) Linearizing around the uniform saddle replaces one internal leg by δGj, and summing over e ∋i and j ∈e \ {i} yields δΣi ∝P j KijδGj.
